pradeep|Chemistry|0|82|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The names of the two nucleic acids state the answer:
**DNA** = **deoxy**ribonucleic acid ⟹ the sugar is **2-deoxyribose**
**RNA** = ribonucleic acid ⟹ the sugar is **ribose**
and in both the sugar is present as the **β-D** anomer in a furanose ring. So, in the order
asked for — DNA first, then RNA:
**β-D-2-deoxyribose, β-D-ribose** ✓ — option (b)
The prefix **deoxy-** means an oxygen is missing, and the **2** says which one: the hydroxyl
at **C-2′** is replaced by a plain hydrogen. That single difference is the whole structural
distinction between the two sugars.
Its consequence is large. The free 2′-OH of RNA can attack the neighbouring phosphodiester
bond, so **RNA hydrolyses readily**, especially in alkali. DNA, lacking that hydroxyl, is far
more **stable** — exactly what is needed of a molecule that must preserve genetic information
unchanged for a lifetime, while RNA is made and destroyed continually.
The distractors are built on the two things that can go wrong: the **order** (option c has
them the right way round for RNA and DNA but reversed for the question as asked) and the
**'2-'** (options a and d write 'deoxyribose' without the locant, which is not a defined
sugar — 3-deoxyribose would be a different compound).
∴ β-D-2-deoxyribose, β-D-ribose.

Note: the printed key gives (d), which pairs an unspecified 'deoxyribose' with
2-deoxyribose and leaves RNA without its ribose. DNA contains 2-deoxyribose and RNA ribose,
so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (b).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|97|Pradeep Chemistry:
Determining the **C-terminal** residue of a polypeptide calls for a quite different reagent
from the one used at the N-terminal, and the question is testing that distinction.
**(a) Hydrazine** ✓ — the method is **hydrazinolysis**. Heating the peptide with anhydrous
hydrazine cleaves every peptide bond and converts **all** the residues into their
**hydrazides** — except the one at the C-terminal, whose carboxyl group is free and which is
therefore released as the **free amino acid**. Isolating and identifying that single free
amino acid identifies the C-terminal residue ✓
The other reagents all work at the **N-terminal** or not at all:
**(c) 2,4-Dinitrofluorobenzene** ✗ — this is **Sanger's reagent**, which labels the **free
α-amino group** at the N-terminal. On hydrolysis the N-terminal residue comes out as a yellow
DNP-amino acid. It was the reagent Sanger used on insulin, and it answers the opposite
question.
**(b) 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine** ✗ — Brady's reagent, for detecting **aldehydes and
ketones**, nothing to do with peptides.
**(d) 3,5-Difluoronitrobenzene** ✗ — not a standard reagent; the fluorine is in the wrong
position to be displaced by an amino group.
(The enzymic alternative at the C-terminal is **carboxypeptidase**, which chews residues off
one at a time from that end.)
∴ hydrazine.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|5|Pradeep Chemistry:
An **antacid** neutralises or suppresses excess stomach acid. Three of the four do; one does
something quite different.
**(c) Aluminium hydroxide** ✓ is an antacid — a weak base that neutralises HCl directly:
Al(OH)₃ + 3HCl ⟶ AlCl₃ + 3H₂O
**(b) Ranitidine** and **(d) Cimetidine** ✓ are also antacids, though of a cleverer kind. They
are **H₂-receptor antagonists**: rather than neutralising the acid already secreted, they
block the histamine receptors on the stomach wall and so stop the acid being produced in the
first place. That makes them far more effective than the old neutralising powders, which
merely treat the symptom and can provoke a rebound.
**(a) Phenelzine** ✗ **not an antacid** — this is the answer. Phenelzine, sold as **Nardil**,
is an **antidepressant**, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor. It raises the level of noradrenaline
and serotonin in the brain by blocking the enzyme that destroys them, and has nothing to do
with the stomach.
The trap is the *-idine* ending shared by ranitidine and cimetidine, which makes phenelzine
look like the odd one out by name as well — and here, unusually, the name is a reliable
guide.
∴ phenelzine.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|9|Pradeep Chemistry:
Take the four drugs one at a time.
**(i) Ranitidine** ⟶ **(s) Antacid.** An H₂-receptor antagonist that blocks histamine at the
stomach wall and so suppresses acid secretion. Sold as Zantac.
**(ii) Nardil (phenelzine)** ⟶ **(p) Antidepressant.** A monoamine oxidase inhibitor; it
blocks the enzyme that destroys noradrenaline and serotonin, raising their levels in the
brain.
**(iii) Chloramphenicol** ⟶ **(q) Antibiotic.** A broad-spectrum antibiotic, effective
against typhoid, dysentery and meningitis.
**(iv) Dimetane (brompheniramine)** ⟶ **(r) Antihistamine.** An H₁-receptor blocker used
against allergy and hay fever.
So the matching is **(i)-(s), (ii)-(p), (iii)-(q), (iv)-(r)** ✓ — option (b).
The fifth entry, **(t) analgesic**, is a decoy with no partner.
The pairing worth pausing on is ranitidine against brompheniramine, because **both are
antihistamines** in the strict pharmacological sense. They act at different receptors —
ranitidine at **H₂** in the stomach, brompheniramine at **H₁** in the tissues — and it is the
receptor, not the chemistry, that decides what the drug is used for. That is why ranitidine
is classed by its effect, as an antacid, and brompheniramine by its effect, as an
antihistamine.
∴ (i)-(s); (ii)-(p); (iii)-(q); (iv)-(r).
pradeep|Chemistry|0|12|Pradeep Chemistry:
An **analgesic** relieves pain without causing unconsciousness. Three of the options are
**antibiotics**, which fight bacteria and have nothing to do with pain.
**(c) Novalgin** ✓ — the brand name of **metamizole** (analgin, dipyrone), a
**non-narcotic analgesic** and antipyretic, used for pain and fever.
The others:
**(a) Streptomycin** ✗ — an antibiotic from *Streptomyces griseus*, historically the first
effective treatment for tuberculosis.
**(b) Chloromycetin** ✗ — the trade name of **chloramphenicol**, a broad-spectrum antibiotic.
**(d) Penicillin** ✗ — the first antibiotic, discovered by Fleming, narrow-spectrum and
bactericidal.
Analgesics divide into two classes worth keeping apart:
**Non-narcotic** — aspirin, paracetamol, ibuprofen, novalgin. They relieve pain without
addiction or loss of consciousness, and most also reduce fever and inflammation.
**Narcotic** — morphine, codeine, heroin. These are opioids: powerful, used for severe
post-operative or terminal pain, and habit-forming.
The *-mycin* and *-cillin* endings are a reliable signal of an antibiotic, which disposes of
three options at a glance.
∴ Novalgin.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|14|Pradeep Chemistry:
A **hypnotic** is a drug that induces **sleep** — a stronger effect than a tranquilliser,
which merely calms.
**(b) Amytal** ✓ — the trade name of **amobarbital**, a **barbiturate**. Barbiturates are the
classic hypnotics: derivatives of barbituric acid that depress the central nervous system
and, in sufficient dose, produce sleep. The family is easy to recognise by its names —
**Veronal, Luminal, Seconal, Amytal** — all ending in *-al*.
The others are not hypnotics and not even drugs of the same kind:
**(a) Seldane** ✗ — the trade name of **terfenadine**, an **antihistamine** for allergy. It
was in fact valued for being **non-sedating**, the opposite of a hypnotic.
**(c) Aspartame** ✗ — an **artificial sweetener**, a dipeptide methyl ester, not a drug at all.
**(d) Prontosil** ✗ — the first **sulpha drug**, an antibacterial, and historically important
as the compound that opened the sulphonamide era.
Barbiturates are now largely replaced by the safer benzodiazepines, because the dose that
induces sleep is uncomfortably close to the dose that stops breathing — and because they are
strongly habit-forming.
∴ Amytal.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|15|Pradeep Chemistry:
**Histamine** ✓ is the chemical that stimulates the secretion of pepsin — and, more
importantly, of hydrochloric acid — in the stomach.
It acts on the **H₂ receptors** of the parietal cells of the stomach wall, and when those
receptors are occupied the cells pour out acid and the chief cells release pepsin. Histamine
is also the mediator of allergic reactions elsewhere in the body, acting there on **H₁**
receptors to cause the familiar inflammation, itching and nasal congestion.
The other three options are all drugs that **oppose** histamine, which is what makes them
tempting:
**(a) Antihistamine** ✗ — the general term for a drug that blocks histamine; by definition it
does the opposite of stimulating secretion.
**(b) Cimetidine** ✗ and **(d) Zantac** (ranitidine) ✗ — both are **H₂-receptor antagonists**.
They sit in the H₂ receptors without activating them, so histamine cannot get in, and acid
secretion falls. They are the standard treatment for hyperacidity and ulcers.
The distinction between the two receptor types is the key idea here. An ordinary
antihistamine for hay fever blocks **H₁** and has no effect on the stomach; a drug for
hyperacidity must block **H₂** specifically. Recognising that there were two kinds of
histamine receptor was what made ranitidine possible, and it earned James Black a Nobel
Prize.
∴ Histamine.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|16|Pradeep Chemistry:
Check each molecule for a sulphur atom.
**(a) Cimetidine** — contains a **thioether** sulphur in its side chain, –CH₂–**S**–CH₂–,
linking the imidazole ring to the rest of the molecule ✗ contains S
**(b) Ranitidine** — likewise contains a **thioether** sulphur, –CH₂–**S**–CH₂–, joining the
furan ring to the chain ✗ contains S
**(d) Saccharin** — its full name is **o-sulphobenzimide**, and the ring contains an
**–SO₂–** group. The sulphur is part of the five-membered ring itself ✗ contains S
**(c) Histamine** ✓ **contains no sulphur** — this is the answer. Its formula is **C₅H₉N₃**:
an **imidazole** ring bearing a –CH₂CH₂NH₂ side chain, made up of carbon, hydrogen and
nitrogen only.
The pattern is worth noticing. Both H₂-blockers, cimetidine and ranitidine, were designed
by modifying the **histamine** molecule so that it would occupy the receptor without
activating it — and in both cases the chemists inserted a **sulphur atom** into the chain.
The natural messenger has none; the synthetic antagonists do.
Saccharin's sulphur is unrelated, belonging to a sweetener rather than a drug, and is there
to make the fourth option.
∴ Histamine.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|18|Pradeep Chemistry:
A **broad spectrum** antibiotic acts on a wide range of bacteria, both **Gram-positive and
Gram-negative**; a **narrow spectrum** one acts on a single group.
**(d) Penicillin-G** ✓ **not broad spectrum** — this is the answer. Natural penicillin G
(benzylpenicillin) is effective almost entirely against **Gram-positive** bacteria, and is
the textbook example of a **narrow spectrum** antibiotic.
The reason lies in the bacterial envelope. Penicillin blocks the enzyme that cross-links the
peptidoglycan of the cell wall. **Gram-positive** bacteria have a thick, exposed
peptidoglycan layer, so the drug reaches its target. **Gram-negative** bacteria carry an
extra **outer lipopolysaccharide membrane**, and penicillin G cannot cross it.
The others are classed as broad spectrum:
**(b) Ampicillin** — a **semi-synthetic** penicillin, modified at the side chain with an amino
group that lets it penetrate the Gram-negative outer membrane
**(c) Ofloxacin** — a fluoroquinolone, active against both groups
**(a) Vancomycin** — a glycopeptide, listed here among the broad spectrum agents
The contrast between penicillin G and ampicillin is the point of the question. They differ
by one small group on the side chain, and that difference turns a narrow-spectrum drug into
a broad-spectrum one — which is exactly why the semi-synthetic penicillins were developed.
Amoxycillin belongs to the same family and is likewise broad spectrum.
∴ Penicillin-G.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|19|Pradeep Chemistry:
A **narrow spectrum** antibiotic is effective against a limited range of organisms — usually
either Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria, but not both.
**(b) Penicillin G** ✓ — the natural penicillin, benzylpenicillin. It acts almost exclusively
on **Gram-positive** bacteria, and is the standard example of a narrow-spectrum antibiotic.
The reason lies in the bacterial envelope. Penicillin works by blocking the enzyme that
cross-links the peptidoglycan of the cell wall. **Gram-positive** bacteria have a thick,
exposed peptidoglycan layer, so the drug reaches its target easily. **Gram-negative** bacteria
have an extra **outer lipopolysaccharide membrane** outside the wall, and penicillin G
cannot cross it.
The other three are **broad spectrum**:
**(a) Chloramphenicol** — acts on both groups, used against typhoid and dysentery
**(c) Ampicillin** and **(d) Amoxycillin** — **semi-synthetic** penicillins, modified at the
side chain with an amino group that lets them penetrate the Gram-negative outer membrane
So ampicillin and amoxycillin differ from penicillin G by a single substituent, and that
substituent is exactly what converts a narrow spectrum into a broad one — which is why those
drugs were made.
∴ penicillin G.

Take each drug class and find its example.
**(a) Antacids** ⟶ **(iii) Cimetidine.** An H₂-receptor antagonist that blocks histamine at
the stomach wall and so suppresses acid secretion.
**(b) Antihistamines** ⟶ **(iv) Seldane.** The trade name of terfenadine, an H₁-blocker used

Three statements are true and one is not.
**(b) Disinfectants harm living tissues** ✓ **true.** That is precisely what distinguishes them
from antiseptics: a disinfectant is applied to **inanimate** surfaces — floors, drains,
instruments — because it is too harsh for skin.
**(c) A 0·2 % solution of phenol is an antiseptic while 1 % acts as a disinfectant** ✓ **true**,
and a good illustration of the point that the **same substance** can be either, depending
only on **concentration**.
**(d) Chlorine and iodine are used as strong disinfectants** ✓ **true.** Chlorine at about
0·2 to 0·4 ppm sterilises drinking water, and both are powerful oxidising germicides.
**(a) Dilute solutions of boric acid and hydrogen peroxide are strong antiseptics** ✗ **not
true** — this is the answer. Both are genuine antiseptics, but they are **mild**, not strong.
Dilute boric acid is weak enough for an eyewash, and dilute hydrogen peroxide is used on
minor cuts precisely because it is gentle on tissue. Calling them **strong** is the error.
The general distinction to carry away:
**antiseptic** — applied to **living** tissue (Dettol, tincture of iodine, dilute H₂O₂)
**disinfectant** — applied to **non-living** surfaces (1 % phenol, bleaching powder)
and the dividing line is often a matter of concentration rather than of substance.
∴ statement (a).
pradeep|Chemistry|0|24|Pradeep Chemistry:
A mixture of **chloroxylenol and terpineol** is **Dettol**, and it acts as an **antiseptic** ✓.
The two components do different jobs:
**Chloroxylenol** (4-chloro-3,5-dimethylphenol) is the active germicide — a chlorinated
phenol that kills bacteria by disrupting their cell membranes and denaturing their proteins.
**Terpineol** is a terpene alcohol which helps dissolve the chloroxylenol, carries it into
the tissue and gives the preparation its characteristic smell.
An **antiseptic** is applied to **living tissue** — cuts, grazes, skin before surgery — and
must therefore kill microorganisms without damaging the tissue itself. That is exactly what
Dettol is for, and it is why the chloroxylenol is used at low concentration: phenols are
powerful germicides, but at higher strength they become **disinfectants**, too harsh for skin.
The other options name quite different kinds of drug:
**(b) antipyretic** — lowers fever (paracetamol, aspirin)
**(c) antibiotic** — kills bacteria **inside** the body, taken internally (penicillin)
**(d) analgesic** — relieves pain (aspirin, morphine)
The familiar observation that Dettol turns milky in water is worth a word: the chloroxylenol
is not water-soluble, so it comes out of solution as a fine emulsion when the alcohol-based
concentrate is diluted.
∴ antiseptic.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|26|Pradeep Chemistry:
Dettol is a mixture of **chloroxylenol** and **terpineol**, so the two compounds A and B must
be those — and the π-electron counts decide which is which.
**A has 6 π-electrons** ⟹ an **aromatic benzene ring**, whose delocalised sextet is exactly
six π electrons. That is **chloroxylenol** (4-chloro-3,5-dimethylphenol), a substituted
phenol.
**B has 2 π-electrons** ⟹ a **single carbon-carbon double bond**, which contributes one π
bond and therefore **two** π electrons. That is **terpineol** ✓ — a terpene alcohol with one
C=C in its ring and no aromatic character at all.
So B is **terpineol** — option (b).
The other options:
**(c) Chloroxylenol** ✗ is compound **A**, with the six π electrons. The question asks for B,
so reading it carelessly gives this answer.
**(a) Bithional** ✗ is an antiseptic added to soaps, but it is not a component of Dettol — and
it contains two aromatic rings, so twelve π electrons.
**(d) Chloramphenicol** ✗ is an antibiotic, taken internally, not an antiseptic component.
The π-electron count is a neat way of distinguishing an **aromatic** component from an
**aliphatic** one without drawing either structure, and that is all the question requires.
∴ terpineol.
